title: Who Is This? The Face Set Toward Jerusalem
sum: Jesus sends the Twelve to announce the kingdom and heal, and Herod, hearing of it, asks the question that runs through the chapter: who is this? Jesus feeds five thousand in a lonely place near Bethsaida. Then, after praying, he asks the disciples who they say he is, and Peter answers, "God's Messiah." At once Jesus tells them that the Son of Man must suffer, and that anyone who follows him must pick up his cross every day.

On the mountain the disciples see his glory and hear the voice: "This is my Son, the Chosen One. Listen to him!" Moses and Elijah talk with him about the exodus he will complete in Jerusalem. Below, he frees a boy the disciples could not help, predicts his betrayal again, and corrects their quarrel about rank. Then, at 9:51, he fixes his face on Jerusalem. A Samaritan village refuses him, James and John want to call down fire, and three would-be followers learn what following costs.
readings: Read as the answer to Herod's question

Herod asks, "Who is this?" (9:9). The crowds guess John, Elijah, an ancient prophet (9:19); Peter says God's Messiah (9:20); the voice on the mountain says God's Son, the Chosen One (9:35). Each answer is truer than the last, and each is corrected by what follows: the Messiah must suffer, and the chosen Son must be heard when he speaks of the cross. Luke arranges the chapter so that the reader learns who Jesus is before the journey to his death begins.
Read as the turning point of Luke

Many scholars see 9:51 as the hinge of the whole Gospel. Up to here Jesus works in Galilee; from here, for ten chapters, he travels toward Jerusalem, teaching his disciples on the way. The chapter gathers the themes of the first half (mission, feeding, healing, Herod) and opens those of the second (the journey, Samaria, the cost of discipleship). The word "exodus" (9:31) gives the journey its meaning.

The Twelve are sent out with power (9:1), yet below the mountain they cannot help a boy (9:40). They confess the Messiah (9:20), yet they do not understand his suffering (9:45), argue about rank (9:46), try to stop an outsider (9:49) and want to burn a village (9:54). Luke does not hide their failures; he shows how much they still had to learn before Acts.

views.H: Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee and Perea, had killed John at Machaerus (Josephus, Antiquities 18.116–119) and now hears of Jesus. Bethsaida, just across the Jordan in Philip's territory, was rebuilt as Julias. The mountain is not named; tradition from the 300s points to Mount Tabor, many scholars to Mount Hermon. Galilean pilgrims often traveled through Samaria to Jerusalem, and clashes between Samaritans and Galileans are recorded under the governor Cumanus around AD 52 (Josephus, Antiquities 20.118–136).
views.C: Luke follows Mark 6:7–44 and then skips to Mark 8:27, leaving out Mark 6:45–8:26 (the "great omission"). He polishes Mark's style, corrects "king" to "tetrarch," replaces "Rabbi" with "Master" and "Amen" with "truly," and adds prayer (9:18, 28–29), "every day" (9:23) and the exodus conversation (9:31). From 9:51 he leaves Mark for a long section built mostly from sayings shared with Matthew (often called Q) and his own material (L). Most critical scholars think the journey is Luke's literary framework rather than a single historical trip.
views.L: The chapter turns on faces: Jesus' face changes as he prays (9:29), he fixes his face on Jerusalem (9:51), sends messengers before his face (9:52), and the Samaritans refuse him because his face is going toward Jerusalem (9:53). The "two men" of the mountain return at the tomb and the ascension (24:4; Acts 1:10). Luke frames the journey with "taken up" (9:51) and the ascension (24:51; Acts 1:2), and his Jesus refuses Elijah's fire, as Elijah himself was taken up.
views.J: Elijah and Moses, the two great figures of Israel's hope, appear with Jesus; the voice repeats Moses' promise of a prophet whom Israel must hear (Deuteronomy 18:15). Feeding in the wilderness recalls the manna and Elisha's loaves. The quarrel with the Samaritans was a dispute between two peoples who both claimed the heritage of Israel, over Jerusalem and Gerizim. Burying one's father was among the most binding duties of Jewish life, which is why Jesus' words in 9:60 shocked.
views.T: The Feast of the Transfiguration (August 6) is kept by Orthodox, Catholic and Anglican churches and in some Lutheran calendars, while many Lutherans keep the Transfiguration on the last Sunday after Epiphany; in Orthodox teaching the light of Tabor is God's uncreated glory (see the card at Mark 9). "Pick up his cross every day" has shaped Christian devotion from monastic rules to Thomas a Kempis' The Imitation of Christ. The rebuke of James and John (with the words added in later manuscripts, "You do not know what spirit you belong to") has often been cited against using force in the name of religion.

deep.b:
With 9:51 Luke begins the longest section of his Gospel: about ten chapters in which Jesus is "on the road" to Jerusalem. Luke reminds the reader of the journey again and again (13:22; 13:33; 17:11; 18:31; 19:11; 19:28) and ends it when Jesus sees the city and weeps over it (19:41–44). Yet the route is hard to trace: after leaving Galilee he is still between Samaria and Galilee in 17:11, and the visit to Martha and Mary (10:38) seems, from John 11:1, to belong near Jerusalem. Most of the material in these chapters is teaching: parables found only in Luke (the good Samaritan, the lost son, the rich man and Lazarus), sayings shared with Matthew and placed differently there, and meals and debates with Pharisees.

Scholars read the section in several ways. Hans Conzelmann saw it as a theological construction: Jesus' journey to suffering, with geography serving theology. C. F. Evans and David Moessner traced parallels with Deuteronomy, where Moses teaches Israel on the way to the promised land; Moessner reads Jesus as the prophet like Moses whose "exodus" (9:31) leads to his death in Jerusalem. Others see a collection of teaching for disciples, arranged around a journey because discipleship means following. Most agree that "the road" in Luke is more than a route: in Acts the followers of Jesus are called "the Way" (Acts 9:2).

deep.h: What Luke does with the transfiguration
deep.b:
Luke's account follows Mark 9:2–8 but changes it in ways that show his interests. Jesus goes up "to pray," and the change comes "while he was praying" (9:28–29). Luke avoids the word "transformed" and speaks instead of his face, recalling Moses' shining face (Exodus 34:29). Only Luke tells what Moses and Elijah talked about: his exodus to be completed in Jerusalem (9:31). Only Luke says the disciples were heavy with sleep but kept awake, or woke fully, and saw his glory (9:32). The voice calls him "the Chosen One" (9:35), linking him to the servant of Isaiah 42:1. And Luke leaves out the conversation about Elijah on the way down (Mark 9:9–13).

The result ties the mountain to the journey that starts in 9:51. Glory and suffering are not two stages that follow each other; the glory is seen while the talk is of his death. For how the churches understand the light on the mountain, see the card at Mark 9:2–3; for the scene's background in Sinai, see Matthew 17.

deep.title: Claude's theory: fire refused, Spirit given in Samaria
deep.b:
In 9:52–55 a Samaritan village refuses Jesus because his face is set on Jerusalem, and John, with his brother, wants fire from heaven to consume it. Jesus refuses. Luke's second volume brings the story back: after Jerusalem, after the cross and resurrection, "Samaria had welcomed the word of God" (Acts 8:14), and the apostles send Peter and John, who pray for the Samaritans to receive the Holy Spirit (Acts 8:14–17). The same John who once asked for fire comes down on Samaria a second time, now bringing the fire of the Spirit (compare 3:16; Acts 2:3). I suggest Luke meant this pairing: Samaria could not receive Jesus while his face was going toward Jerusalem, but it receives him once Jerusalem's events are done, and the disciple who wanted judgment becomes the minister of the gift.

The pairing of 9:54 with Acts 8 is widely noted in studies of Luke-Acts (Robert Tannehill's Narrative Unity of Luke-Acts, for one). What this box adds is only the claim that Luke designed the pair on purpose, through the figure of John. It rests on Luke's habit of setting scenes in his Gospel and in Acts side by side (Talbert's "literary patterns").

echoes: Mark 6:7–44; Mark 8:27–9:40; Matthew 10:1–14; Matthew 14:1–21; Matthew 16:13–28; Matthew 17:1–23; Matthew 18:1–5; Matthew 8:19–22; Exodus 16; Exodus 24:15–18; Exodus 34:29–35; Deuteronomy 18:15; Psalm 2:7; Isaiah 42:1; Isaiah 50:7; 2 Kings 1:9–12; 2 Kings 2:9–11; 2 Kings 4:42–44; 1 Kings 19:19–21; Acts 1:9–11; Acts 8:14–17; 2 Peter 1:16–18

settings.what: The charge to the Twelve
settings.to: The Twelve, as he sends them out to the villages of Galilee
settings.when: After his own preaching tour with them (8:1), before Herod hears of the mission Mark 6:7–11 gives a shorter form of the charge. Matthew 10:5–42 makes it a long discourse to the Twelve that also forbids Gentile and Samaritan towns (Matthew 10:5), while Luke soon has Jesus send messengers into a Samaritan village (9:52).
settings.why: To send them as he himself was sent: carrying nothing, depending on the welcome of those who receive the kingdom, and leaving a clear sign against towns that refuse. The bare equipment makes the messengers part of the message: God provides, and the kingdom does not come by wealth or force.
settings.readers: Luke's first readers, Theophilus and the churches of Gentile and Jewish believers he wrote for (on who they were and when Luke wrote, see the book introduction), knew traveling missionaries such as Paul and Barnabas, who shook the dust off their feet at Pisidian Antioch (Acts 13:51). The charge showed them the pattern of their own mission, and Luke later shows Jesus changing it for a harder time (22:35–36).

settings.what: Herod's question
settings.to: No hearers are named; Luke reports what he said, presumably at his court
settings.when: As reports of Jesus' work and of the Twelve's mission reach him
settings.why: Herod's words show both his fear and his guilt: he killed John, and now a prophet like John has appeared. His question, "Who is this?", is the question the chapter answers. In Mark 6:16 and Matthew 14:2 Herod decides that Jesus is John raised, and both go on to tell how John died; in Luke Herod only asks, and the story of John's death is left out.
settings.readers: Readers who knew that Herod would meet Jesus at his trial (23:6–12) heard the ruler of Galilee asking the question they could answer.

settings.what: The Twelve's request and Jesus' orders at the feeding
settings.to: Jesus, then the Twelve, near Bethsaida with a large crowd
settings.when: Late in the day, in a lonely place Mark 6:32–35 and Matthew 14:13–15 set the meal in a lonely place reached by boat, and Mark sends the disciples on to Bethsaida afterward (Mark 6:45); Luke sets it near Bethsaida itself (9:10).
settings.why: The Twelve want the crowd sent away to fend for themselves; Jesus tells them to feed the people and organizes the meal. Having just been sent out with nothing, they learn again that what they have is enough in his hands.
settings.readers: Readers who broke bread in their homes (Acts 2:42) heard the actions they knew from the Lord's Supper (22:19): he took, blessed, broke and gave.

settings.what: The question about who he is, and the first prediction of his death
settings.to: The disciples, privately, after Jesus had been praying
settings.when: Right after the feeding, in Luke's order Mark 8:27 and Matthew 16:13 set the question on the road near Caesarea Philippi, after events Luke leaves out (Mark 6:45–8:26); Luke drops the place and sets it at prayer.
settings.why: To draw from the disciples a confession of who he is, and at once to correct what "Messiah" means: the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected by the leaders in Jerusalem, be killed and be raised. The order of silence keeps the title from being heard as a call to revolt.
settings.readers: Readers who confessed Jesus as the Messiah who had suffered and been raised learned from the scene that this was the plan from the start (24:26, 46).

settings.what: Sayings on the cross and the coming glory
settings.to: "All": the disciples, and in Luke's wording anyone who would follow
settings.when: Immediately after the first prediction of his death Mark 8:34 has Jesus call the crowd together with his disciples, and Matthew 16:24 has him speak to the disciples alone; Luke's "to them all" opens the saying to anyone.
settings.why: To make plain that following him means the same road he takes: daily self-denial, readiness to lose one's life, no shame about him or his words, with the promise of the kingdom and his coming glory.
settings.readers: Readers in a church that faced rejection and sometimes death learned from Luke's "every day" that the cross is also a daily discipline.

settings.what: Peter's words and the voice from the cloud
settings.by: Peter, then God speaking from the cloud
settings.to: Jesus, Moses and Elijah (Peter's words); Peter, James and John (the voice)
settings.when: On the mountain, as Moses and Elijah were leaving Only Luke says Jesus went up to pray and that Peter spoke as the men were leaving; Mark 9:2 and Matthew 17:1 date the scene "after six days," Luke "some eight days" (9:28).
settings.why: Peter wants to hold on to the moment by building booths; the voice answers by naming Jesus as God's Son and Chosen One and commanding the disciples to listen to him, as Israel was told to listen to the prophet like Moses.
settings.readers: Readers who saw Moses and Elijah, the Law and the Prophets, give way to Jesus heard God's own word about the one they followed and the command to listen to him.

settings.what: The rebuke of a faithless generation
settings.to: The crowd, the boy's father and the disciples who failed
settings.when: Coming down from the mountain the next day Mark 9:14–19 sets the rebuke amid an argument between the disciples and some scribes, which Luke leaves out; Matthew 17:17 and Luke both have "warped," which Mark lacks.
settings.why: To name the unbelief around him, including the disciples' failure, in words that echo Moses' complaint about Israel (Deuteronomy 32:5), and then to show that God's power is not limited by it.
settings.readers: Readers who knew failure in their own ministries saw that Jesus' power did not depend on his followers' strength.

settings.what: The second prediction of his betrayal
settings.to: His disciples, while the crowd was still marveling
settings.when: Right after the healing of the boy Mark 9:30–31 and Matthew 17:22 set the prediction later, as they traveled through Galilee, and Mark's Jesus keeps that journey secret; Luke ties it to the crowd's amazement.
settings.why: To set the crowd's amazement in its place: the one whose power they admire is about to be handed over. The disciples are told to keep the words in their ears even though they cannot yet understand them.
settings.readers: Readers who knew how the story ended understood that the disciples' blindness was lifted only by the risen Jesus (24:45).

settings.what: The child at Jesus' side
settings.to: The disciples, who had been arguing about who ranked highest
settings.when: Right after the second prediction Mark 9:33–37 sets it in a house at Capernaum, after the disciples had argued on the road. In Matthew 18:1–5 the disciples themselves ask who is greatest, and the saying opens a long discourse on life in the community.
settings.why: To overturn their idea of greatness: the one who welcomes the least, a child, welcomes Jesus and the Father, and the smallest is the great one.
settings.readers: Readers in house churches, where rank and honor mattered as much as anywhere in Roman society, would hear the saying again at the Last Supper (22:24–27).

settings.what: John and the outsider exorcist
settings.to: Jesus (John's report); John and the others (Jesus' answer)
settings.when: Right after the teaching on the child Mark 9:38–41 has the scene in the same place and adds the saying about a cup of water; Matthew does not have it.
settings.why: To correct a group spirit that tries to control the use of Jesus' name. Anyone not against them is on their side.
settings.readers: Readers who knew other groups and teachers acting in Jesus' name outside their circle (Acts 18:24–26; Acts 19:1–7, 13–16) needed both generosity and discernment.

settings.what: The offer of fire and Jesus' rebuke
settings.to: Jesus (their offer); James and John (the rebuke)
settings.when: After a Samaritan village refuses to receive Jesus, at the start of the journey to Jerusalem Only Luke has this scene.
settings.why: The brothers want to act like Elijah and destroy the village; Jesus refuses to answer rejection with violence. His mission is not to destroy those who refuse him.
settings.readers: Readers who knew that Samaria later received the word (Acts 8), and who knew Jesus' teaching to love enemies (6:27–36), saw him refuse to answer rejection with fire.

settings.what: Three would-be followers
settings.to: Jesus (their offers and requests); each man (Jesus' answers)
settings.when: On the road, as the journey to Jerusalem begins Matthew 8:18–22 has the first two exchanges in Galilee, before the crossing of the lake, with a scribe and with one of the disciples; the third (9:61–62) is only in Luke.
settings.why: To show the cost of following: no home, no delay even for the holiest family duties, no looking back. The answers are deliberately sharp, to show that the kingdom comes first.
settings.readers: Readers who had left home and family for the gospel, and others still weighing what it would cost, found the outcome left open, so that each must answer for himself.
views: The sayings set out what every disciple owes Jesus: first loyalty, above home and family (14:26).
Some scholars read them as aimed at those who left everything to travel with Jesus and later as missionaries, not at every believer (compare Theissen's "wandering charismatics").

title: Sent Out Like Lambs: Neighbors and Guests
sum: Jesus sends out seventy-two more messengers in pairs, ahead of him, with a charge much like the Twelve's: travel light, bring peace to the houses that welcome you, eat what you are given, heal the sick, announce that the kingdom of God has drawn near. He grieves over the Galilean towns that saw his acts of power and did not repent. The messengers come back full of joy that even demons obey them; Jesus, who saw Satan fall like lightning, tells them to rejoice instead that their names are written in heaven. Then, in the Holy Spirit, he thanks the Father for showing these things to little children.

A lawyer asks what he must do to inherit eternal life and answers his own question from the law: love God, and your neighbor as yourself. "And just who is my neighbor?" Jesus answers with the story of a man left half dead on the Jericho road, passed by a priest and a Levite and rescued by a Samaritan, and turns the question around: who became a neighbor? The chapter ends in a home, where Martha serves and Mary sits at Jesus' feet, and Jesus says Mary has chosen the one thing needed.
readings: Read as a chapter about welcome

Hospitality ties the chapter together. The messengers depend on welcome (10:5–8) and leave a sign against towns that refuse it (10:10–12). A Samaritan, from the people who had just refused Jesus a welcome (9:53), takes in a wounded stranger and pays for his lodging (10:34–35). Martha welcomes Jesus into her house (10:38). Jesus is both guest and host: he receives welcome, and his word is the best food served (10:39, 42).
Read as two great commandments in action

Many interpreters, from Augustine to modern commentators, read 10:25–42 as the lawyer's two commandments shown in two scenes: the Samaritan shows love of neighbor, Mary at Jesus' feet shows love of God. Neither cancels the other; the Samaritan acts and Mary listens, and both are praised.
Read as an allegory of salvation

From Origen and Augustine to the Middle Ages, the parable was read as the story of salvation: the traveler is Adam, the robbers the devil and his angels, the priest and Levite the Law and the Prophets that could not save, the Samaritan Christ, the inn the church, the innkeeper the apostle, and the Samaritan's return the second coming. Most modern scholars set this reading aside as foreign to the question Jesus was answering, though some (and many preachers) still find in the Samaritan a picture of Christ, who came to his enemies and paid for their healing.

views.H: Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum lay within a few miles of each other at the north end of the Sea of Galilee. The road from Jerusalem down to Jericho drops more than 3,000 feet in about 17 miles through desert and was known for robbers. Priests and Levites served in the temple in turns and lived in towns around the country. Samaritans and Jews were bitter rivals, with violence on both sides in the first century (Josephus, Antiquities 18.29–30; 20.118–136). Women like Martha could own and run households.
views.C: The sending of the seventy-two is found only in Luke, but its charge overlaps Matthew 10 and Mark 6 so closely that most scholars think Luke has two versions of the mission instructions, one from Mark (9:1–6) and one from the sayings source he shares with Matthew (often called Q). 10:13–15 and 10:21–24 also come from that source (Matthew 11:21–27; Matthew 13:16–17). The question about the great commandment is in Mark 12:28–34 and Matthew 22:34–40, but Luke's form, with the lawyer giving the answer and the parable following, differs greatly. The good Samaritan and Martha and Mary are Luke's own material (L).
views.L: Luke sets the parable between two questions about eternal life and neighbors, and ends both scenes with a command to act: "Keep doing this" (10:28) and "do the same yourself" (10:37). The Samaritan's actions mirror the robbers' in reverse: they stripped, beat and left him; the Samaritan bandages, carries and stays. The chapter moves from a crowd of seventy-two to one lawyer to one household, from the many to "one thing" (10:42).
views.J: The lawyer's summary of the law, love of God and neighbor, had Jewish precedent (Testament of Issachar 5:2, in a work of debated date; Philo), and Jesus approves it. Other Jewish teachers summed up the law through love of neighbor: Hillel, a generation before Jesus, with the negative golden rule (Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a), and later Akiva, who called Leviticus 19:18 a great principle of the Torah (Sifra). Amy-Jill Levine argues that the parable is not about Jewish law blocking mercy: Jewish law required help for an abandoned body, and the hearers would have expected an ordinary Israelite after the priest and Levite. The shock is the Samaritan, the enemy who proves to be the neighbor. Readings that make the priest and Levite stand for a heartless Judaism have done real harm.
views.T: The Orthodox Church commemorates the Seventy Apostles (January 4), naming among them figures such as Luke, Mark and Barnabas. The good Samaritan has given its name to hospitals, laws and charities, and has been painted by Rembrandt and Van Gogh. Martin Luther King Jr., in his last speech (Memphis, 3 April 1968), retold it, saying the priest and Levite asked, "If I stop to help this man, what will happen to me?" while the Samaritan asked, "If I do not stop to help this man, what will happen to him?" Martha and Mary became the classic picture of the active and contemplative lives (see the card).

deep.h: The good Samaritan through the centuries
deep.b:
Origen reports that "one of the elders" read the parable as a picture of salvation: the man going down is Adam, Jerusalem is paradise, Jericho the world, the robbers hostile powers, the priest the Law, the Levite the Prophets, the Samaritan Christ, the inn the church (Homilies on Luke 34). Augustine gave a fuller version, in which the innkeeper is the apostle Paul (Questions on the Gospels 2.19). This reading ruled preaching for a thousand years and is still heard; it has the strength of seeing Christ as the one who comes to his enemies and pays for their healing.

Since the 1800s most interpreters have read the parable first as Jesus' answer to the lawyer: love has no borders, and the neighbor is the one who acts. Twentieth-century readers stressed the Samaritan as the hated outsider. Amy-Jill Levine and others have pressed further: the parable is not "Judaism versus compassion," since Jewish law and Jewish hearers knew the priest should stop; it is a story about an enemy who shows mercy, which forces the hearer to ask whether he could accept help from, and learn from, the people he despises. Martin Luther King Jr.'s retelling made it a call to risk safety for others.

The short scene has been read in strikingly different ways. For Augustine, Martha's serving belongs to this life and passes away, while Mary's listening is the life of heaven already begun (Sermons 103–104). For much of the medieval church, Mary stood for the contemplative life of monks and nuns, Martha for the active life, and Thomas Aquinas taught that the contemplative life is better in itself, citing this verse (see the card). Meister Eckhart reversed the usual reading and praised Martha as the more mature of the two, one who could work without losing God.

Modern readers often see Mary as a woman claiming the place of a disciple, sitting at a teacher's feet, with Jesus defending her right to learn. Feminist scholars disagree about whether Luke liberates or restrains: Elisabeth Schüssler Fiorenza argues that Luke prefers a silent, listening woman to an active one whose diakonia recalls the ministry of leaders. Others note that Jesus does not condemn Martha's service, only her anxiety, and that in Luke serving is the work Jesus himself takes on (22:27). The text holds both: the one thing needed is to hear his word, and service flows best from it.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the chapter of guests
deep.b: From 9:51 to 10:42 every scene turns on welcome. A Samaritan village refuses Jesus as a guest (9:53). Jesus himself "does not have anywhere to rest his head" (9:58). The seventy-two go out as guests who must not move from house to house (10:5–8), and towns are judged by how they receive them (10:10–16). Then the roles turn: a Samaritan becomes the host of a stranger, paying the innkeeper (10:34–35), and Martha becomes Jesus' host, only to learn that he is the one who serves the best portion (10:42). I suggest Luke built this run of scenes as a deliberate answer to 9:53: the Samaritans who would not host Jesus are answered by a Samaritan host in a story, and the homeless Son of Man is welcomed in a woman's house. Hospitality readings of Luke are well developed (Brendan Byrne, The Hospitality of God; John Koenig, New Testament Hospitality), and they take in these scenes. What this box adds is only the claim that 9:51–10:42 was built as one cycle answering 9:53.

echoes: Matthew 9:37–38; Matthew 10:7–16; Matthew 10:40; Matthew 11:21–27; Matthew 13:16–17; Matthew 22:34–40; Mark 6:7–13; Mark 12:28–34; Genesis 10; Genesis 19; Numbers 11:16–29; Isaiah 14:12–15; Psalm 91:13; Deuteronomy 6:5; Leviticus 18:5; Leviticus 19:18; Leviticus 19:34; 2 Chronicles 28:15; John 11:1–2; John 12:1–3; 1 Timothy 5:18; 1 Corinthians 10:27; Acts 8:5–25

settings.what: The charge to the seventy-two
settings.to: The seventy-two, sent in pairs ahead of him to the towns on his way
settings.when: At the start of the journey to Jerusalem, soon after the Samaritan village refused him (9:53) Matthew puts these sayings in the charge to the Twelve (Matthew 9:37–38; Matthew 10:7–16, 40), and Mark 6:7–11 has a shorter form of that charge; only Luke has a second sending.
settings.why: To prepare the towns for his own coming. As with the Twelve, the messengers go defenseless, bring peace, depend on hospitality, heal and announce the nearness of the kingdom; their reception is a town's response to Jesus and to God (10:16).
settings.readers: Luke's first readers, Theophilus and the churches he wrote for (on who they were and when Luke wrote, see the book introduction), knew a church sent to the nations (24:47; Acts 1:8). The number seventy-two, the nations of Genesis 10 in the Greek Bible, may have told them that this second sending looked ahead to theirs. Paul refers to the Lord's command behind its saying about the worker's pay (1 Corinthians 9:14), and 1 Timothy 5:18 cites the saying beside Scripture.
views: The seventy-two stand for the mission to all nations after the Twelve's mission to Israel (Luke's arrangement of 9:1 and 10:1).
Luke had two forms of the mission charge, from Mark and from Q, and gave each its own sending (most critical scholars).

settings.what: Woes on Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum
settings.to: The towns of Galilee, addressed as if present, in the hearing of the seventy-two
settings.when: Within the charge to the seventy-two; Matthew 11:20–24 places the woes after John's question, as a separate reproach
settings.why: To warn that seeing God's acts of power brings responsibility. Towns that saw the most and did not repent will fare worse at the judgment than the Gentile cities the prophets condemned.
settings.readers: Readers who knew that much of Galilee had not followed Jesus, while Gentiles were receiving the gospel, learned that privilege without repentance is no protection.

settings.what: The report of the seventy-two and Jesus' reply
settings.to: Jesus (their report); the seventy-two (his reply)
settings.when: On their return from the mission Only Luke has the return and this reply.
settings.why: To interpret their success: their exorcisms are signs of Satan's fall and of the authority Jesus has given them. But to keep them from pride in power, he directs their joy to what God has done for them: their names are written in heaven.
settings.readers: Readers who knew the signs and wonders of the apostles in Acts needed the warning that power is not the ground of joy or of salvation.

settings.what: Jesus' prayer of thanks to the Father
settings.by: Jesus, rejoicing in the Holy Spirit
settings.to: God the Father, in the hearing of the disciples
settings.when: In the same hour as the seventy-two returned Matthew 11:25–27 has the prayer "at that time," after the woes on the towns of Galilee, with no returning mission.
settings.why: To praise the Father for revealing the kingdom to "little children," the unlearned disciples, rather than to the wise, and to state the unique relationship of Father and Son through which that revealing happens.
settings.readers: Readers who were mostly ordinary people, few of them wise or powerful by the world's standards (1 Corinthians 1:26), heard their own calling in the prayer.

settings.what: The private blessing of the disciples
settings.to: The disciples, privately
settings.when: Right after the prayer Matthew 13:16–17 has the blessing in the parable chapter, to explain why the disciples understand when others do not.
settings.why: To tell the disciples what a privilege they have: they are seeing and hearing what prophets and kings longed for, the time of fulfillment.
settings.readers: Readers who had not seen Jesus themselves, but received the witness of those who had (1:2), found that the blessing reached them through it.

settings.what: The lawyer's question about eternal life
settings.by: A lawyer (an expert in the Torah), with Jesus' replies
settings.to: Jesus, in the hearing of the disciples and others
settings.when: On the journey, soon after the return of the seventy-two Mark 12:28–34 and Matthew 22:34–40 set a similar exchange in the temple courts during Jesus' last week in Jerusalem: there the question is which commandment comes first, and Jesus gives the answer himself. Luke sets it early in the journey, the question is about eternal life, and the lawyer answers. Many scholars think Luke moved Mark's scene here to lead into the parable; others think Jesus was asked such questions more than once.
settings.why: The lawyer tests Jesus' teaching on the central question of the law. Jesus sends him back to the Torah he knows and approves his answer: love God fully and your neighbor as yourself, and keep doing it.
settings.readers: Readers among the Gentiles learned that Jesus affirmed the heart of Israel's law, and that its double commandment remained the way of life for his followers.
views: "To test him" means the lawyer hoped to trap Jesus or show him up (as in 11:53–54).
Jewish teachers tested one another's learning in debate; the lawyer may have been probing, not plotting (compare the friendly scribe of Mark 12:28–34).

settings.what: The parable of the good Samaritan
settings.to: The lawyer who asked "who is my neighbor?", with others listening
settings.when: Right after the lawyer's question, on the way to Jerusalem Only Luke has the parable.
settings.why: To answer the lawyer's question by changing it: not "whom must I love?" but "who acted as a neighbor?" A Jewish hearer is made to see mercy in a Samaritan, the enemy, and is told to do the same. The parable breaks down the borders the lawyer wanted to draw around his duty.
settings.readers: Readers in churches where Jews, Samaritans and Gentiles were learning to call each other neighbors (Acts 8; Acts 10) received a model of love across hostile lines.
views: The Samaritan is a model to imitate; the point is the command "do the same yourself" (most modern interpreters).
The Samaritan is Christ, who rescues fallen humanity (Origen, Augustine and much later preaching).
A story about receiving help from the enemy
The hearer identifies with the man in the ditch and must accept rescue from a Samaritan (Funk, Crossan, Levine in different ways).

settings.what: Jesus' answer to Martha
settings.to: Martha, in her house, with Mary listening
settings.when: During his visit, when Martha asks him to tell Mary to help Only Luke has this scene; John 11:1 and John 12:1–3 place the sisters at Bethany, near Jerusalem.
settings.why: To free Martha from anxious busyness, not to belittle her welcome, and to defend Mary's choice to listen to him: one thing is needed, and it will not be taken from her.
settings.readers: Readers who met in houses, often hosted by women (Acts 12:12; Acts 16:15), and who were working out how serving and hearing the word fit together (Acts 6:1–4), learned that hearing Jesus comes first.

traditions.q: Does "Whoever hears you hears me" (10:16) give the church's leaders a lasting teaching authority?
views: Yes. Christ's words to his apostles pass to their successors, the bishops with the pope, so that the faithful receive their teaching with docility as Christ's own (Catechism 87, quoting this verse; Lumen Gentium 20). This authority serves the Word of God and is not above it (Dei Verbum 10).

The authority belongs to the church as a whole, guided by the Holy Spirit; bishops teach in succession from the apostles, and their teaching is confirmed when councils are received by the whole people of God. The faithful hear Christ in the church's living tradition.

Bishops and pastors are to be heard as Christ when they preach the gospel; the Augsburg Confession cites this verse for that duty. But when they teach against the gospel, the churches have God's command not to obey them (Augsburg Confession 28).

The verse honors the ministry of the Word: when Scripture is faithfully preached, Christ speaks, so that "the preaching of the Word of God is the Word of God" (Second Helvetic Confession 1). The authority lies in the Word, not in the office; Calvin applies the verse to the minister's faithful teaching.
The apostles' authority now reaches us in the written Scriptures, the supreme standard by which all teaching and every church is judged; no later office holds it (1689 London Confession 1).

traditions.q: "Keep doing this, and you will live" (10:28): can anyone gain eternal life by keeping the commandments?
views: With God's grace, the commandments can and must be kept; the Council of Trent condemned the saying that they are impossible for the justified to keep. Eternal life is both a grace promised to God's children and a reward for good works done in grace (Trent, Session 6, chapters 11 and 16).

Salvation is union with God, received as gift and lived in cooperation with grace (synergy). Love of God and neighbor is not a way to earn life but the very life of the age to come, begun now through the sacraments and the struggle of obedience.

Jesus answers the lawyer with the law: perfect love of God and neighbor does lead to life, but no sinner can do it, so the law shows sin and drives to Christ, who kept it for us. Law and gospel must be kept distinct (Formula of Concord, Article 5).

The law truly promises life to perfect obedience, but since no one renders it, the promise serves to convict and send us to Christ; Calvin comments that Jesus speaks here in terms of the law, not of the gospel (Calvin on Luke 10:28).

traditions.q: Has Mary "picked out the good share" (10:42) by choosing a life of contemplation over active service?
views: The contemplative life is in itself higher than the active, as Thomas Aquinas taught citing this verse, though the best life joins them, handing on to others what is contemplated (Summa Theologiae II–II, questions 182 and 188). Augustine read Mary's part as the life of heaven begun now. Religious orders of contemplatives are honored on this basis.

Mary and Martha picture two ways that belong together in the Christian life; the monastic tradition of prayer of the heart (hesychasm) values stillness at the Lord's feet, but all believers are called to prayer and to service.

The verse does not rank callings. The Augsburg Confession rejects the claim that monastic life is a higher state of perfection; Mary's good share is faith that hears Christ's word, open to every Christian in every calling (Augsburg Confession 27).

Calvin says the passage has been twisted to praise a contemplative life withdrawn from duty; Christ commends Mary for hearing his word, not for idleness, and does not condemn Martha's service, only her distraction (Calvin on Luke 10:38–42).
